subject: On incommensurate units and scale: CR and other analyses

messages.subject: On incommensurate units and scale: CR and other analyses
parts:
Grant et al.,

 

Grant’s original question concerned application of a particular method (the CR) for his data, which contained both continuous and meristic count data. However, the real issue is not a ‘failing’ of a particular method to handle someone’s data, but rather rests in the logic of asking mathematics to do something it cannot. This issue pertains much more broadly to quantitative analysis in general, and since we receive queries that boil down to this issue several times a year, it is time to revisit this discussion again. 

 

With all multivariate analyses, one must have data of commensurate types, of commensurate units, and in commensurate scale. Otherwise, the analysis is simply GIGO.  The reason is that multivariate analyses ultimately ask about the locations of objects in a multivariate dataspace: their similarity and difference, the trait correlation and covariation, etc.  That requires a distance measure (recall that covariances and distances are intimately related mathematically: see Gower 1966: so even if the analysis is about trait correlations/covariances, mathematically this is asking about distances [albeit of variables]). So only data of commensurate types can be combined for a multivariate analysis.

 

As an example, say one has a binary trait (0/1), meristic counts (1,2,3), and a continuous variable. Technically all of these variables contain numbers, so surely one can perform a principal components analysis on them right?  WRONG! (well, one could, but one should not).  Binary traits are in a dataspace defined by Hamming distance (or another binary distance measure), counts are in a space of Gower distances, and continuous data may be in a space defined by Euclidean distance.  It makes no biological or mathematical sense to combine these and try to understand similarity of differences among objects; the math simply does not work.

 

Importantly, this issue can even occur when one has all continuous variables. Say we have temperature, elevation, and relative humidity. Surely we can obtain an ordination to show similarities amongst localities?  Well…. Maybe, but not in their original units. Temperature (C), elevation (m), relative humidity (g/m^3) are in incommensurate units and scale. So what does a covariance mean in this context? How does one interpret (deviations in C * deviations in g/m^3)? One cannot. Same thing with a distance, which is also based on those deviations. And for some of these variables (temperature), once could use other units that convey the same relative information but stretch that axis; which in turn stretches a sub-dimension of the dataspace. Not good. Now commensurate units could be obtained from continuous variables if they are converted to their standard normal deviates; and in this case they could be combined. However, in their original units/scale they should not (and standard normal deviates will not resolve the issue of different data types: binary, meristic, continuous).

 

If one ponders their particular discipline (ecology, evolutionary biology, psychometrics, anthropology, etc.), I’m sure one can come up with many published examples of the above infractions. Put simply, errors of this type abound in many quantitative disciplines. But being aware of this is important so as not to repeat these same errors. Such spaces simply cannot be interpreted mathematically or biologically, meaning the resulting ordination, MANOVA, CR, etc. cannot be interpreted. For a discussion of these in the context of dataspaces and ordination see: Legendre and Legendre, 2012 (ecology side) and Adams and Collyer, 2019 (evolution side).

 

Folks, one must understand that this is not a failing of a method or even of mathematics. It is simply asking math to do something it cannot. One cannot interpret combined datasets when those variables are of incommensurate type, units, or scale. Complicated workarounds could be envisioned, but are well beyond the general scope of discussion; and these have not been fully vetted  mathematically to demonstrate that they do what is intended.

 

The short answer is: just don’t do it.

 

Best,

 

Dean

Unfortunately, this dataset includes meristic and continuous data for traits that we know are correlated and face similar selection pressures, in at least some contexts. If there is an analogous method that can accommodate both data types that I am unfamiliar with, I would gladly use that instead. But this seemed to be an instance where providing caveats to an imperfect application of the test was a less misleading option than excluding data due to the absence of a perfectly suitable test.

I have an update on this if anyone else runs into this issue. I tested whether things were going wrong because I was using na.omit within the function by using it instead to create a new list of dataframes (one for each lake) without missing values or unused variables. Then I ran that through the function.

 

here is that new code: 

lapply(split.adj.data,function(x){

  modularity.test(x,c('a','a','a','a','a','a','a','b','b','b','c','c','c','c','c','d','d','d'),CI=T)
})

It turns out that na.omit wasn't the issue, and the presence of missing values wasn't either.

 

What did cause problems were two vectors of data describing meristic traits within one of the partition groups (which included a total of 7 variables). Within some lakes, neither of those two meristic traits varied at all, and in those lakes, removing one or both of those variables produced normal modularity.test results.

 

I am still not sure of the specific problem given that leaving in one but not both of these non-varying traits produces normal results, but this is a step in the right direction, I guess.

 

Grant

Hi all,

 

I am using modularity.test() to test for modularity of non-landmark variables in fish within a few different lakes. For all of the lakes, I get results that mostly make sense, but the tests in some of the lakes return NaN as the effect size. They all return CRs, CIs, and p-values, so I can't figure out why effect sizes would be NaN. N ≥ 10 for all lakes, and I've tried this just for individual lakes without using lapply() with the same result. I have also done the same test across all lakes without issue. Any thoughts?

 

here is my code (I can send the data if necessary):

 

split.adj.data<-split(adj.data,adj.data$Lake, drop = F)
lapply(split.adj.data,function(x){
  modularity.test(na.omit(x[,c(3:17,22:24)]),c('a','a','a','a','a','a','a','b','b','b','c','c','c','c','c','d','d','d'),CI=T)
})
